title: Eight Weeks of Asking God Why
subtitle: An eight week plan from James Bell for anyone asking why God would let this happen. Job, the laments, and the cross, walked slowly, with no tidy answers and no hurry.
intro:
This is an eight week walk for the person asking why God would let this happen, and asking it from inside the suffering. It is also for the skeptic who asks the same question as an argument. This plan comes from a pastor who was an atheist first, and it will not treat that argument as a small one. Each week holds one focus, one small daily practice, one thing to read, one tool to use, and one honest question. The weeks go slowly through Job, the lament psalms, and the cross, because those are the places where Scripture stays longest with pain. No tidy explanation waits at the end, since the Bible never gave one to Job. What the weeks offer instead is harder to put in a sentence and sturdier over time: a God who lets the question be asked to his face, who rebuked the friends who explained too much, and who did not keep his distance from suffering.

It is not a cure, and it is not a substitute for a doctor, a licensed counselor, a pastor, or the people who will sit with you in this. Walk it at whatever pace your life allows. A missed week is not failure, you just pick it back up when you can, and some weeks you may manage only the question at the end. That counts. If the suffering outlasts these eight weeks, it does not mean you walked them wrong. Job's book runs forty-two chapters, and God does not answer him until the thirty-eighth.
careNote: Suffering that brings despair, or that has taken your sleep, your appetite, or your ability to work, needs a doctor or a licensed counselor as well as a pastor, and asking for that help is faith, not failure. In a crisis, call or text 988.

weeks.why: Something has happened, or is still happening, and one question will not leave you alone: why would God let this happen? You may have been told, gently or not, to stop asking it. Scripture keeps the question on the lips of its most faithful people. David asks how long four times in two verses (Psalm 13:1-2), Job asks why through most of a long book, and Jesus asks why from the cross. If you come to it as an argument, it is a serious one, and it deserves a hearing at full strength. So the only task this week is to ask it honestly and let it stand, because a question hurried toward an answer tends to come back later, and heavier.
weeks.practice: Each day, write the question in your own words, exactly as it comes, without making it more polite than it is. Under it, write one plain sentence about what actually happened. That is the whole practice. You are not looking for an answer this week, only telling the truth about the question.

read.label: Suffering and the Silence of God, the problem of pain without the easy answers

tool.label: The care page for this question, so you know where real help is before you need it

weeks.reflection: When I ask why, what am I really asking God for: a reason, a rescue, or some sign that he is there?

weeks.focus: Job, who would neither curse God nor pretend
weeks.why: Job loses his wealth, his children, and his health, and the book is plain that he did nothing to deserve it. What he does next holds together two responses we usually keep apart. He falls to the ground and worships, and the narrator says, "In all this, Job did not sin or charge God with wrongdoing" (Job 1:22). Then, after his friends have sat with him in silence for seven days, he curses the day he was born (Job 3). He never curses God, and he never pretends. Scripture keeps the worship and the cry side by side, and the narrator does not rebuke him for the cry. If you have been allowed only the first, this week you are allowed the second.
weeks.practice: Read Job 1 to 3 across the week, a portion each day, aloud if you can. Notice both of Job's responses, the worship in chapter 1 and the cry in chapter 3, and write down which one you have been allowed and which one you have hidden. If Job's words in chapter 3 sound like your own nights, tell someone today, and in a crisis call or text 988.

read.label: The Study Bible on Job 1, with its history and the hard question of why God allowed the test

tool.label: The Prayer Generator, choose Prayer in Suffering for the days your own words run out

weeks.reflection: Have I believed that crying out to God and trusting him cannot live in the same person, and where did I learn that?

weeks.focus: The friends who explained too much
weeks.why: Job's friends begin well. They sit on the ground with him for seven days and say nothing, because they can see how great his pain is (Job 2:13). Then they start to explain, and every explanation is a version of the same one: God is just, so suffering must be deserved. Much of what they say is true as a general rule, and all of it is wrong about Job. Job names what is driving them: "you see terror, and you are afraid" (Job 6:21). At the end God says to Eliphaz, "you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has" (Job 42:7). We still reach for their explanations for the same reason, and pastors like me reach first.
weeks.practice: Each day, write down one thing someone has told you about your suffering, or one thing you keep telling yourself, such as that everything happens for a reason or that you must have deserved this. Beside it, write whether it is true, whether it is actually in Scripture, and whether it helped you or mostly helped the person saying it.

read.label: The Study Bible on Job 4, where Eliphaz says many true things and still speaks wrongly of God

tool.label: The topical Scripture reference, open Suffering to see how Job and Romans 8:28 are commonly misused

weeks.reflection: Which explanation of my suffering have I accepted because it was easier than silence, and is it true?

weeks.focus: Lament, the faith that stays in the room
weeks.why: Psalm 13 complains and pleads for four verses and then, without saying that anything has changed, turns to trust. Psalm 88 never turns. It ends in the dark, on the line "darkness is my closest companion" (Psalm 88:18). Yet it opens by calling God "the God of my salvation" (Psalm 88:1), and it keeps speaking to him all the way down. That is what lament is: complaint addressed to God himself by someone who has not stopped believing he can hear. The church kept these prayers for the nights when nothing else is honest enough, and many of us were never taught to pray them.
weeks.practice: Pray Psalm 13 aloud each morning. On one evening, when you are ready, pray Psalm 88 slowly and let it end where it ends. Then write a lament of your own in four parts: name God, tell him what is wrong, ask for what you want, and add a line of trust only if it is true today. If Psalm 88 has become the only prayer you can pray, tell a pastor, a doctor, or a counselor this week.

read.label: The Study Bible on Psalm 88, the one lament that never turns to hope, and why it was kept

tool.label: How to Practice Lament, with a four-part pattern for writing a lament of your own

weeks.reflection: Have I been speaking about God in my suffering more than I have been speaking to him?

weeks.why: Some of what makes suffering unbearable was never Christian teaching at all. Christianity never claimed that suffering is always a punishment you earned; Jesus refused that reading of a disaster in Luke 13. Nor does it call the evil thing secretly good, since Scripture names death an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26). And nowhere does it promise that you will be told why in this life. Job never was. Faithful Christians still differ over how directly God's hand is in a particular sorrow, and you don't have to settle that to keep praying. What they hold in common is that God is good, that he is not the author of evil, and that evil will not have the last word.
weeks.practice: Each day, finish this sentence honestly in a notebook, I have believed that my suffering means. Then hold what you wrote up against this week's reading. Cross out whatever Christianity never claimed, and keep whatever survives. By the end of the week, write one sentence about God that you can still say honestly.

read.label: The Hard Questions page, opened at Why does God allow suffering and evil, on what Christianity does and does not say

tool.label: The theodicy page, five attempted answers to the problem of evil at full strength, none offered as a cure for grief

weeks.reflection: Which of my fears about this suffering come from what Christianity actually claims, and which come from something I was handed along the way?

weeks.why: When God finally speaks from the whirlwind, he never mentions the scene in heaven and never gives Job a reason. He asks where Job was when the foundations of the earth were laid (Job 38:4), and he walks him through the sea, the snow, the stars, and the mountain goats giving birth. Some readers hear only power overwhelming a grieving man, and that objection deserves to be felt. But listen to what Job says at the end: "My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You" (Job 42:5). He never received an explanation. He received God himself, and it changed him.
weeks.practice: Read Job 38 to 42 across the week, a chapter or so a day, and notice what God says and what he never says. Then sit in silence for ten minutes, not asking why, only asking him to come near. If the silence stays silent, stay in it anyway. Write down one thing you noticed, even if it was only that you stayed.

read.label: The Study Bible on Job 38, where God answers from the whirlwind, and the hard question of why he does not explain

tool.label: Where Is God When It Hurts, a five-session study to walk with one friend, its third session on Job and the whirlwind

weeks.reflection: If God gave me himself but never the reason, would that be enough, and if not, what am I still asking him for?

weeks.focus: The cross, where God entered suffering
weeks.why: It is natural to picture God above suffering, untouched by it, handing down reasons or withholding them. Christianity makes a stranger claim: in Jesus, God came into suffering himself, all the way to death. On the cross Jesus prays the opening line of a lament psalm, "My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1), so the deepest why in Scripture is spoken by the Son of God. The cross leaves your suffering unexplained, and it also means that wherever this takes you, you are not going anywhere God has not already been.
weeks.practice: Read Mark 15 slowly each day this week, and on one of those days read Isaiah 53 beside it. Each time you reach verse 34, pause and pray that line as your own. Then sit for two minutes with this: the prayer you just prayed has already been prayed by the Son of God.

read.label: The Study Bible on Mark 15, the crucifixion and the cry of forsakenness from the cross

tool.label: The Deep Bible Study Companion, choose Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12, the suffering servant, and read it beside Mark 15

weeks.reflection: What changes in how I pray if God has not watched suffering from a distance but carried it himself?

weeks.why: Christian hope is sturdier than optimism, and more honest than the claim that all of this will turn out to have been fine. It rests on an event, the resurrection of the same Jesus who cried out on the cross, and it does not skip the groaning. Read Romans 8:18-28 whole and you find creation groaning, believers groaning, and the Spirit interceding "with groans too deep for words" (Romans 8:26) before Paul says that God works all things together for good. Read there, verse 28 calls nothing evil good; it promises that God is at work in all of it for his people. The Bible's last pages keep the tears in view to the end, with the promise that God "will wipe away every tear from their eyes" (Revelation 21:4). A hope that admits the tears can be trusted with them.
weeks.practice: Read Romans 8:18-28 slowly each day, and on the last day read Revelation 21:1-5. Before the week ends, write on a card the psalm you will keep praying, the person you will keep telling the truth to, and the promise you are holding, and put it where you will see it each morning. The suffering may outlast these weeks. The card is for that.

read.label: The Study Bible on Romans 8, with the hard question of whether verse 28 means everything that happens is good

tool.label: How to Find Hope When Nothing Changes, a daily practice to keep after these weeks end

weeks.reflection: What am I actually hoping for now, and would that hope still stand if nothing in my circumstances changed?
